items.title: Ordinal Bounty #0: 100,000 sats for a single sat whose ordinal ends with a 0
items.text:
Ordinal numbers are serial numbers for satoshis. In an effort get people interested, I've been offering bounties on specific ordinals, or ordinals with specific qualities. I had a huge grab bag of bounties, but I decided to change it up and focus on one bounty at a time.

The current bounty is [here](https://ordinals.com/bounties)!

To claim the bounty, send a single sat* to the address on the bounty page. The catch: The sat must be the first sat in the output you send. This is stipulated because otherwise, sending at least 10 contiguous sats would be sufficient to claim the bounty, and that would be too easy.

To claim the bounty, you'll have to understand [how ordinals work](https://github.com/casey/ord/blob/master/bip.mediawiki), look up some ordinals you own on the [ordinals.com block explorer](ordinals.com) and write some pretty simple code to construct a transaction with input sand outputs in the right order.

NB Whenever you look up a utxo you own on a block explorer, it's a privacy leak! You can run your own copy of the block explorer, get the code [on github](https://github.com/casey/ord).

The reward is 100,000 sats**.

The bounty can only be claimed once, and is definitely unclaimed as long as no transactions have been sent to the bounty address.

The bounty page contains instructions on how to claim the bounty.

If anyone claims this bounty, I'll come up with another, harder one. Maybe one day the bounty will be to find one of the [three](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′336″0‴) [epic](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′672″0‴) [ordinals](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′1008″0‴) mined so far.

\* In practice you'll have to send more, so your transaction doesn't have dust outputs, and thus be non-standard and not relayed.

items.title: Resolvr: a Bounty Marketplace that takes the Agent out of Escrow
items.text:
Recently, a popular bounty marketplace, BountySource, [stopped paying out bounties](https://github.com/bountysource/core/issues/1586) to developers. Many users reported outstanding or significantly delayed payouts.  [[1](https://github.com/bountysource/core/issues/1539)] [[2](https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/issues/5900)]. The entities or persons running BountySource likely misused the escrowed funds being held for bounties.  Bounty posters and developers have been searching for an alternative. 

But the risk of exit scams or insolvency are inherent to all centralzied escrow agent.  That's why most jurisdictions place onerous fiduciary duties on escrow agents to faithfully hold funds for safekeeping and deliver them according to the terms of the deal.   But it can take time and money to get compensation through the courts and usually recovery is for pennies on the dollar. The costs of legal action outweighs any bounty amounts lost through embezzlement.   

So some existing platforms, like Algora, don't bother with escrow.  But, as one former BountySource user [pointed out](https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/issues/5900#issuecomment-1771603383), that just shifts the trust to the bounty grantor.

![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/65395e3087238f2bcef5379f/9d1297aa-6072-41b9-bea3-a57814b2dee1/more+trust+in+donor.png?content-type=image%2Fpng)

Replit provides a bounty marketplace that does escrow bounty funds, but payouts are not instant or free.  Users are awarded Replit's token (cycles) for solving bounties, and must request payout in USD by email.  Users are charged a 25% withdrawal fee for any bounty funds earned, and there is a minimum withdrawal amount of $350. So, not only are you trusting that Replit won't go bankrupt, you are paying through the nose for that risk. 

[Resolvr](https://www.resolvr.io) takes the centralized agent out of escrow.  It doesn't control or possesses the bounty funds.  Instead, Resolvr leverages bitcoin's native programmability to attest to whether the bounty has been solved, triggering payout automatically.  This removes the need to trust the platform or grantor.

And Resolvr doesn't decide whether the bounty has been solved;  a panel of crowdsourced developers performs the review.   

Resolvr is the first bounty marketplace to offer dependable escrow and payouts, as well as transparent dispute resolution.  Oh, and it's cheaper than the existing alternatives.

You can [sign up](https://www.resolvr.io/) to be an alpha tester today! And check out the [GitHub](https://github.com/Resolvr-io) and join the conversation on [discord](https://discord.gg/DsqRw8My4m).

items.title: TABConf 8 - The last TABConf
items.text:
After many incredible years, TABConf 8, taking place October 12-15, 2026, in Atlanta, will be the final TABConf.

[https://tabconf.com](https://tabconf.com)

TAB began as a meetup in 2016 and became a conference in 2018 as the community grew. From the beginning, TABConf focused on the technical side of Bitcoin and helped fill a gap left by events like Scaling Bitcoin.

Today, that gap is much smaller. There are now many strong technical Bitcoin conferences, workshops, and BitDevs communities. That is a good thing.

TABConf was never built as a business. It has always been a volunteer-run community service supported by a small core team and a much larger group of contributors.

The goal was simple: keep it technical and avoid price talk, hype, and "wen moon" content.

TABConf was not the place to learn why Bitcoin matters. It was the place to come once you understood that and wanted to learn what to do next. It has always been a conference for builders and doers.

We believe true sovereignty requires some level of technical competence. Better tools matter, but users also need the knowledge and confidence to take responsibility for their own money. With that being said do to the recent coldcard hacks we will have additional focuses on secure self-custody, including multisig, multiple vendors, and reducing single points of failure. We will also provide highly hands-on help and training for attendees who need support setting up and safely using these systems.

TABConf has always emphasized learning by doing through workshops, villages, puzzles, and interactive formats rather than relying only on panels and presentations.

A special thank you goes to everyone over the years that have helped, especially Brandon Iglesias, who has worked on TAB with me for 10 years and helped make TAB and the conference what it became. His idea to organize TABConf openly through GitHub also made the event unique.


TABConf has led to friendships, jobs, projects, companies, and even marriages. That impact is difficult to measure, but it means more than I can properly express.

Let's send it off the right way.

We hope you will join us in Atlanta for the final TABConf. Tickets, sponsorships, and additional information are available on the TABConf website.

items.title: Wasabi Wallet is unstoppable
items.text:
We are proud to announce that Wasabi Wallet v2.8.1 is out. It sets a major milestone which took more than a year to achieve: to make Wasabi unstoppable.

Yes, **Wasabi Wallet is unstoppable** now. This is the result not only of a long, complete redesign but, even more important, of a lesson learnt from the Samourai failure. One day we all woke up with the news about the Samourai case, and what shocked me the most, apart from the human perspective, was witnessing how an open source software project can die. I remember reading users requesting support because their wallet showed them a 0 btc balance, the fear, the ignorance reigning in most of them about what that 0 meant — something I don't want Wasabi users to ever go through.

The latest version can not only work with nothing more than your own node but can also work with just the Bitcoin P2P network. Coordinators form a long chain of fallbacks, releases are distributed automatically thanks to Nostr, and even if GitHub cancels our subscription and blocks the project repo, nothing happens because Wasabi can find the releases wherever we put them.

We could enumerate features — there are lots of them — but **unstoppability** is the one that we would like to highlight today.

To the loyal Wasabi users, all our gratitude for your support and we hope you find this work valuable.

The Four Horsemen
items.text:
<ins>**The Four Horsemen (of the Blockchain):**</ins> A unified spec for Bitcoin coinjoin protocols, combining every existing on chain technology into one incentive compatible, block space efficient, flexible, decentralized implementation.

**Author:** Kruw - npub1pww7030g95nv9ptfpgfu69jpfxj6pm33xxueztsupwekce45wx4sm6en60


**Abstract:** Different approaches have been taken to improve on chain privacy for Bitcoin using the coinjoin primitive. Each technology has unique trade offs and fragmented liquidity. However, a single client that assembles every technology can passively adapt to the user’s needs, access an overlapping liquidity pool, and provide privacy by default with minimal additional fees.


**Subprotocols:**


1. **WabiSabi** - For consolidating UTXOs without revealing common ownership, creating the ZeroLink standard denomination inputs, and privacy maximized spending
2. **ZeroLink** - For block space efficient remixing and DoS protected rounds
3. **JoinMarket** - Provides on demand liquidity for whales, and provides free (or profitable) remixing for low time preference users
4. **PayJoin** - Enhances third party privacy for on demand payments with supporting wallets, block space efficient, steganographic spending


**Strengths, weaknesses, and costs:**


WabiSabi uses keyed verified anonymous credentials and lets users make every spend a coinjoin. The drawback is that it has poor on chain scalability. The flagship WabiSabi implementation (Wasabi Wallet v2.0+) uses \~600-700 vBytes per user, per transaction. There is an additional cost (\~100 sats per tx at 1 sat/vByte) that users must discard to create matching value outputs. Maximum round size is limited by performance (Tor is the bottleneck). Sybil dilution is disincentivized since users pay for their own mining fees. Failure-to-sign DoS protection is enhanced by increasing the minimum value for eligible inputs.

ZeroLink uses Chaumian Blind Signatures and lets users create fixed sized denomination outputs from equal sized or larger sized inputs. The drawback is limited amount flexibility that leaves users with untouchable toxic change that shouldn’t be consolidated. The flagship ZeroLink implementation (Wasabi Wallet v1.1+, now discontinued) used a base denomination of 0.1 BTC. As a piece of the wider spec, ZeroLink costs \~100 vBytes per user, per transaction. Maximum round size is limited by available liquidity. Sybil dilution is disincentivized since users pay for their own mining fees. Failure-to-sign DoS protection is enhanced by only whitelisting WabiSabi outputs for ZeroLink inputs to guarantee a sunk mining fee cost for the attacker.

JoinMarket makers provide liquidity, and takers pay their mining fees when consuming liquidity for coinjoin transactions. The drawback is that the taker is a trusted coordinator that learns the input-output mappings of makers. A JoinMarket coinjoin with 10 makers uses \~4,000 vBytes (makers will create two outputs each, which will eventually lead to consuming two inputs later). Maximum round size is limited by diminishing marginal returns for takers. Sybil dilution is avoided by makers’ commitments to fidelity bonds. UTXO probing is prevented by takers’ commitments to Proof of Discrete Log Equivalence (PoDLE). Failure-to-sign DoS protection is not a concern since makers are altruistic acceptors of taker fees.

PayJoin is an opportunistic coinjoin between senders and receivers that can confuse third party analysis. The drawback is that both counterparties are single points of failure, and wallet/behavioral fingerprints may leak additional information. The payjoin sender subsidizes the mining fee for the receiver’s first input, paying for \~210 vBytes. Failure-to-sign DoS and UTXO probing attacks are prevented by the sender presigning a fallback payment to the recipient. Payjoins are assumed to be “Sybiled” by each counterparty automatically.


**Incentives and UX integration:**


This is a matrix style comparison that shows how the subprotocols complement each other to fix their individual weaknesses.

Users have an incentive to use WabiSabi to enhance privacy before and after ZeroLink coinjoins, and before and after Payjoins. This protocol is capable of providing end to end privacy by itself, but cost-sensitive users will benefit from these integrations:

* ZeroLink enables highly scalable remixing with very low fees
* JoinMarket gives WabiSabi whales access to a huge liquidity pool, and gives passive participants the chance to gain free remixes
* Payjoin gives users a faster and cheaper alternative compared to sending their payment directly in a WabiSabi coinjoin, and Payjoins between WabiSabi users further increase their privacy

Users have an incentive to use ZeroLink in between WabiSabi coinjoins to avoid fees. This protocol provides incomplete privacy by itself, but is made whole with an additional WabiSabi integration:

* WabiSabi gives ZeroLink even sized inputs and handles change outputs from ZeroLink payments, which gives users access to a larger liquidity pool
* JoinMarket gives ZeroLink participants the chance to gain free remixes
* Payjoins between ZeroLink users further increase privacy

Users have an incentive to use JoinMarket in between their other coinjoins to passively enhance privacy. This protocol provides complete privacy by itself, but is extremely costly for the taker initiating it

* WabiSabi is more scalable than JoinMarket, but can be a slow experience for whales
* ZeroLink is less flexible and less liquid than JoinMarket, but is far more scalable
* Payjoins between JoinMarket users further increase privacy

Users have an incentive to use Payjoin when receiving payments in between their other coinjoins. This protocol provides incomplete privacy by itself, but is enhanced by any underlying coinjoin integration:

* WabiSabi can be performed before/after a payjoin to fully protect both users
* ZeroLink can be performed before a payjoin to protect the receiver’s source of funds
* JoinMarket gives Payjoin participants the chance to gain free remixes


A client that fully deploys these tools will be able to abstract away user decisions for how to handle their UTXOs, and perform the necessary privacy operations in the background for each scenario. In order to comply with this spec, wallet synchronization must be performed using compact block filters or the user’s full node **by default.**

Last year, at TABconf, Car & Keyan asked me what I do all day.

With total honesty, I told them I spend much of my time hanging out a bar near me. For some reason, they found this amusing, like I'm wasting my life drowning in drinks.

Well, that problem won't plague me much longer, because the bar is on its last legs. I found out recently that the owner "Craig" is two months behind on paying the landlord, and the doors will likely be locked this coming Monday. It's the end of an era.

**The Bar**

I initially started hanging out at the bar in mid-2023, a few months after its opening. The reasons were primarily out of convenience; it was near home, had comfortable furniture to lounge (sofas and cushioned chairs) and do work (upright seating), large windows allowing the sun to shine through, and great wifi that made it convenient to work away from home. As I spent more and more time there, I got to know the staff and roughly three dozen other regulars that used it as a pseudo workplace and home away from home. If you wanted to see "the crew," that was the default place you'd go. For close to three years, if I wasn't at home or the gym, the bar was the most likely place you'd find me and many others.

The glue of the bar was "Colby." The founding manager, he designed and built the space for Craig (who lives >100 miles away and I've seen maybe twice), running operations, finance, deliveries, hiring and maintenance. Although the staff had turnover, as is typical for any kind of service establishment, Colby and a handful of long-serving bartenders were consistent faces. Everything ran like clockwork, until \~6 months ago, when Colby finally moved on to a higher paying job opportunity. The glue was gone, so to speak, and it seemed like operations slowly began to fall apart without an experienced manager in charge. Staff would mention that they were late in getting their paychecks, certain drinks would be out of stock, and so on. Several other members of the team headed for the exits and regular customers started fading away. I knew the place was hanging on, but I didn't know the severity of the situation until one of the last remaining long-serving bartenders showed me the late rent statement, along with threat of legal action, two days ago.

**Schelling Points and Third Spaces**

Discussing the situation the other night, someone suggested we all start hanging out at a similar bar about 5 minutes away. I immediately knew this wouldn't work because of the difficult shifting the [Schelling Point ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focal_point_(game_theory))(a term bitcoiners might be familiar with). The value of the bar isn't purely drinks and decor, it's the knowledge that, if I show up at this place, there's likely 10-15 people I know hanging out there. The conversation, familiar faces, spontaneous interactions cannot be easily replicated at a new location. Everyone is making the same rough calculation, "I'll go there because everyone else will probably go." Now that the bar is closing, while some might choose hangout spot A, others will switch to B or C or D. There's no effective coordination mechanism to get everyone to choose the same option. Just like money or languages or communication protocols, hangout spots have something of a network effect to them.

In popular discourse, there has been much lamenting about the [decline of third spaces](https://www.aei.org/society-and-culture/americas-third-places-are-disappearing-and-why-it-matters/). Many reasons have been given for this- rising rent costs, economic stress, social isolation- but I think one of the understated factors is that we all have phases of our lives, and periodically move onto the next thing. We move for school, for jobs, for relationships. Few live in their hometowns well into adulthood. Every aspect of life is more transient. The hometown pub that you and your friends hung out at from youth well into old age doesn't really exist anymore.

I don't know if I'll go look for a new bar. Maybe I'll take this opportunity to travel further and sample many different locations, instead of being loyal to one spot (although you don't get the benefits of community, in this case). Or maybe I'll be more productive and get work done at home, without the distractions of laughter and friendship. Only time will tell.

items.title: What’s the difference between a soft fork, a hard fork, and a chain split?
items.text:
This question cropped up a few times lately with some people referring to RDTS as a hard fork attempt. Let me try to define how I perceive the terms to be used in Bitcoin development circles:

#### Soft Fork

A soft fork is a consensus change that is forward-compatible to existing node software. The rules restrict blocks to a subset of what was permitted per the prior rules. Miners need to upgrade to be compatible, otherwise they might include transactions or build blocks that are forbidden per the new rules. Non-mining unupgraded nodes can follow along even if they are unaware of the new consensus rules.

The network will generally coalesce on the new rules, *if a soft fork is enforced by the majority of the hashrate*. If there are any blocks that break the new rules, they are reorganized out by the hashrate majority disregarding them.

#### Hard Fork

A hard fork is a consensus change that breaks forward-compatibility to existing node software. The new rules permit blocks that were rejected as invalid by existing node software. Only upgraded nodes can follow a hard fork, unupgraded nodes are either stuck at the fork height or follow a non-upgraded alternate chaintip.

#### Chain Split

Whenever miners are working on two or more chaintips, we speak of a chain split. This happens organically when two miners find competing blocks at the same height. It also happens when not everyone adopts a hard fork or when a soft fork is supported by a minority of the hashrate and network.

items.title: Research in Public #19:  The Golden Triangle for AI Research Assistants
items.text:
Yay, I finally set up a good research assistant workflow using Cursor Agents.

I got it doing some pretty high effort, high value, but low ambiguity tasks, like data repair.  That seems to be the golden triangle of well-leveraged AI use.

I have a large dataset that collects data from multiple agencies.  Each agency keeps their data in a separate schema.  The provider tries to normalize the data across agencies, but does it really bad job of it.  Thankfully, the provider provides the raw JSON for each record direct from their respective agencies.  The AI seems to do a pretty good job of reading the raw JSON and writing a script to repair the normalized fields.

The cycle goes like this.  Sample broken records from the dataset.  Personally peek into the raw data to see what might be wrong.  If the record seems repairable, give the bot the example and tell it to update the repair script to handle this case.  After just a few iterations, I was able to repair almost 99% of the broken records in the dataset.  For some fields, this meant going from 0% populated to 99% populated.

It's not totally hands off, but figuring out the repair script by hand would probably take me a lot longer, and the AI is smart enough to test a few cases on its own and look for string patterns automatically.  I still need to help it catch and deal with edge cases, but with every iteration the repair script gets better and better.

Also, here are some cursor rules I'm using to silo my data from the agent, and get the agent to keep detailed diaries of its work:

***

* `raw-data-protection.mdc`

```markdown
---
description: Data protection policies 
alwaysApply: true
---

# Raw data protection

- Load `RAW_DATA_PATH`, `MY_DATA_PATH`, and `AGENT_DATA_PATH` from `.env` (via `python-dotenv` in Python, or equivalent).
- **Never** create, modify, delete, move, or overwrite files under `RAW_DATA_PATH` or `MY_DATA_PATH`.
- Treat everything under `RAW_DATA_PATH` or `MY_DATA_PATH` as read-only input.
- As the agent, you may write files to `AGENT_DATA_PATH`.
```

***

* `research-workflow.mdc`

```markdown
---
description: Agent Workflow
alwaysApply: true
---

# Agent workflow

## Agent workspace

- Keep any scripts you generate under `agent/scripts/`
- Do not modify user generated scripts under `scripts/` unless instructed to
- Any artifacts or intermediate datasets generated can be saved to `AGENT_DATA_PATH`

## Agent reports

- After finishing any task, write a report under `agent/reports/`:
- Filename: `agent/reports/YYYY-MM-DD-short-slug.md`
- Describe what was done and the main findings
- Include a summary paragraph at the top
- If any artifacts were generated, list their file locations 
- Keep entries concise and factual
```

***

Lastly, I haven't given up on the Stacker News research project.  I just haven't had much time to work on it after two rejections.  But I plan to keep shopping it around at conferences and journals.  I think the work deserves to be published, even if it doesn't end up at one of the top tier journals.

```
Hello list,

Fidelity bonds could be used to help create trust-minimized federations 
that are needed for things like chaumian ecash servers or sidechains.

 From what I've seen until now, people working on chaumian ecash or 
sidechains say that the federation controlling the multisig keys will be 
based on some kind of reputation. Perhaps it will be some pseudonymous 
nyms that have built up a good reputation over a long time. I suggest 
another option is to use fidelity bonds to decide who gets to control 
the multisig keys.

Fidelity bonds are a way to deliberately sacrifice bitcoin value in a 
way that can be proven to a third party. In practice this is done by 
sending bitcoins to an address which is time-locked using the 
OP_CHECKTIMELOCKVERIFY opcode. The redeemscript and UTXO, along with a 
signature, can be shown to anyone to prove that the sacrifice happened. 
This system has already been deployed in JoinMarket since August 2021, 
and at the time of writing about 600 btc have been locked up, some for 
several years. The whole scheme is similar in some ways to PoW that 
bitcoin itself uses to avoid sybil attacks when solving the double spend 
problem.

It's important to understand what is the value-add of fidelity bonds and 
what it isn't. Fidelity bonds don't solve the trust issue, as someone 
with a big fidelity bond could still steal funds from the ecash server 
or sidechain using multisig keys they control. Such systems will always 
be custodial.

Rather, fidelity bonds strongly incentivize that the different fidelity 
bond owners are actually different people. That might be exactly the 
kind of thing needed for distributing the keys of big multisigs, 
especially now that taproot allows us to create very big multisig 
schemes. This happens because the value of a fidelity bond is calculated 
as a greater-than-linear power of the bitcoin sacrifice. So for example 
if the power was 2, and someone sacrificed 5 bitcoins of value, their 
fidelity bond would be worth 5 x 5 = 25. If instead they sacrificed 6 
bitcoins their fidelity bond would be worth 6 x 6 = 36. This superlinear 
power is what creates a strong incentive for the different fidelity 
bonds to actually be controlled by different people, because anyone 
behaving rationally will put all their bitcoins into just one fidelity, 
not split them up over many bonds. As a sybil attacker needs to 
distribute their bitcoins over many different bonds, they are 
mathematically punished. The fidelity bond system achieves this without 
revealing anything much about those people's identities.

Another value-add of fidelity bonds is they are very much in keeping 
with the cypherpunk ethos, as anyone can create a fidelity bond and 
advertise it in the market. As the bitcoins can be mixed with coinjoin 
before and after sending to the timelocked address, the scheme doesn't 
have to be linked to any identity. Only money talks; not reputation, 
political power or geographical power.

I don't know yet exactly the details of how such a scheme would work, 
maybe something like each fidelity bond owner creates a key in the 
multisig scheme, and transaction fees from the sidechain or ecash server 
are divided amongst the fidelity bonds in proportion to their fidelity 
bond value.

Regards
CB
```

[2022]

items.title: Can we have a serious talk about the LARP in Bitcoin
items.text:
I logged into X for the first time in a while to understand the post-mortem of how Coldcard was able to be attacked and the full extent of the threat. (Reluctantly, I really hate that place.)

Coldcard and Rodolfo Novak (AKA NVK) were supposedly one of the most respected brands / personalities in Bitcoin. The Coldcard was *the machine* you used to generate and secure your precious Bitcoin seed and defend it from an NSA covert ops team, or whatever. 

The Coldcard was supposedly for *Serious People* and was the ultimate solution – everything else was an "inferior piece of shit".

Yet somehow, they were able to fuck this whole thing up so badly. The literal number one thing that a hardware wallet needed to do: to generate and store a secure seed, was botched so badly that $40million worth of BTC was stolen in half an hour.

The flaw in the Coldcard firmware is not obvious and involves the interaction between a few different files and config etc, but still - the error has been sitting right there for years. Some of the more serious people have commented that this thing should have failed safe and not done anything if it wasn't giving true entropy. Others have brought up the controversial move that CoinKite made from open source to "source viewable" - whatever.

I was never impressed by the aggressive and dismissive persona that this guy NVK projected online, however I have never met him in person and recognise that we live in the age of short-form video and algorithmic feeds – so you gotta do what you gotta do for clicks.

But zooming out, it seems that instead of doing all those podcasts and conferences and taking swipes at genuine open-source projects, a serious project would have made sure that their product actually worked.

A real security / cryptography team and a proper business would have isolated that thing, run unit tests, done some sanity checking on the entropy, red-teamed their own system, and had many sets of eyeballs on that code. 

**But the thing failed, and I wonder if it is time for all of us to look in the mirror.**

These kinds of people - and there are more of them out there, had the trust and the respect of a huge swath of hardcore Bitcoin enthusiasts. 

Why?

I think it is because *they talk like a "Bitcoiner" and look like a "Bitcoiner"?*, but really it is a LARP.

There has been so much hate and anger in Bitcoin stirred up lately from these kinds of people, whether from the BIP110 crowd, general bigotry, and even some of the most cherished Bitcoin-only products.

It is all so tiring.

Some of these people are just simple minds. They want an ideology or an easy idea, an "us vs them" that they can play out in their mind and online that feels good. But hard reality is nuanced, economics, money and cryptography are complex topics.

The more nefarious and intellecutually gifted of these people use manipulation and snake oil to charm people into thinking that because "Bitcoin Only" or "no shitcoin inside" or "steak loving / freedom loving" that somehow what they say is right and what they have works properly. They speak the right shibboleths and go on the right podcasts to be anointed as OG.

I am adjacent to this. I am sure I've said some things that were not correct. I have my own [humble podcast](https://thetransformationofvalue.com/) and have met my fair share of "influential Bitcoiners". There are many genuine people out there. I have met some very talented builders and nuanced thinkers. But more often than not those kind of people keep their voice down, they listen, they consider things deeply.

I have also met (or at least seen) my fair share of loudmouths and know-it-all Bitcoin influencers. They want followers - they want legions who will buy their shitty product or invest in their treasury company or something.

I have met their acolytes too, the ones who follow after every podcast, who doomscroll X, who repeat the shibboleths and are quick to use a [No True Scotsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_true_Scotsman) argument against anything that does not align with their prescribed worldview.

I once mentioned to someone like this, the most self-sovereign of all plebs, that I was running a Lightning node - do you know what they told me?

"You know that is a waste of time."

What are they all looking for? Something that gives them an identity in this strange tribe of ours?

What do you even do with freedom once you attain it?

They certainly don't want the detail and nuance and inherent compromise required of our messy fallen world – they don't want the nuance that *Pseudo Random Number Generation* is not the same as *True Random Number Generation*.

I long for essays on economics and political theory, of nuanced debate about elliptic curves that I cannot hope to fully comprehend. I pine for civil debate and actual insight. I thought the [Coldcard post-mortem Block did](https://engineering.block.xyz/blog/predictable-rng-fallback-and-32-bit-reseed-in-coldcard-firmware) was actually great and insightful compared to what Coinkite put out. 

I feel like a bit of that lives on Stacker News and I have a few Bitcoin friends in real life who I can have long walking conversations with and trade viewpoint - but for the most part it is a sea of noise out there.

Whatever the LARP is in Bitcoin, I hope the fallout from Coldcard and the BIP110 washes away at least a bit of it.

– CE

items.title: ColdCard Entropy Bug: An Investigative History
items.text:
**An investigative history into the ColdCard entropy bug**

{:toc}

In comment https://stacker.news/items/1539078/r/SimpleStacker?commentId=1539121, I remarked that the more I looked into the ColdCard situation, the worse it seemed.  @optimism asked me what I was referring to, but I didn't want to divulge at the time, because I wasn't entirely sure if what I was thinking was accurate. I wanted to get my facts and timelines straight. But I investigated, and now I am ready to discuss what I found.

# Background

The core question is when, how, and why the entropy bug entered into ColdCard's firmware.  In CoinKite's own [post-mortem](https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/), they confirmed that the bug was introduced when they migrated away from Trezor-based libraries to `libNgU` for their cryptographic operations.[^1]

![](https://m.stacker.news/150793)

This happened on **March 1st, 2021**, with commit [b18723d](https://github.com/Coldcard/firmware/commit/b18723dddb6d751c39978e4364b56b2414f68b47) in ColdCard's firmware repo.

The bigger question is, *why did they migrate to `libNgU`*?

# Personality conflicts and accusations of copying

Due to all the posts that were surfacing on Stacker News about NVK and ColdCard's past, I came across https://stacker.news/items/172265, where I learned that NVK had gotten into multiple online scraps about proper attribution in FOSS.

In **July 2018**, NVK got into a bit of a scrape with Pavol Rusnak (cofounder of Trezor) about how ColdCard copied Trezor code but renamed it something else.  Rusnak thought they weren't giving proper attribution:[^2]

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1600/1*c0coZp-aiJnDGIPj3W-tGQ@2x.png)

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1600/1*7eb3_4FsfG-sX4nppy9IXw@2x.png)

This by itself isn't really that big of a deal. CoinKite was within its rights to copy Trezor's code, because it was distributed under the GNU GPLv3 license, meaning you can copy the code as long you also distribute your code under the same license.  Rusnak was simply upset about the naming conventions they chose, which removed the word "trezor" from filenames.  But as we'll see, the requirement to distribute under GNU GPLv3 will later play a central role in CoinKite's decision to move away from Trezor-based code.

# Moving off GNU GPLv3

Fast forward two years to **July 2020**.  Foundation Devices forks ColdCard's firmware to make its own *Passport* hardware wallet. This upsets NVK, who accuses them of affinity scamming:

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1600/1*12PhVcEHi9EoEO_TaUzp1Q@2x.png)

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1600/1*4NUnJFW77jCjd8Aolm05TQ@2x.png)

Unhappy that other companies are forking ColdCard's code, he starts thinking about moving to a new license:

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1600/1*Td7uAJ6nQhleDgN8nRCd2w@2x.png)

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1600/1*hNlDtv2_Roi8SZ6JvFUTlg@2x.png)

# The fateful day

On **March 1st, 2021**, commit [b18723d](https://github.com/Coldcard/firmware/commit/b18723dddb6d751c39978e4364b56b2414f68b47) was pushed to ColdCard's firmware library.

The commit message reads `"First pass w/ libNgU"`, and the change log is as follows:

```markdown
## 4.0.0 - , 2021
- Major internal changes! Minimal external change...
    - now using Bitcoin Core's "libsecp256k1" for EC crypto operations
    - super fast pure-assembly AES256-CTR code makes USB communications faster
    - new optimized SHA256 and SHA256(SHA256()) code in use
- HSM/CKBunker mode:
    - users with passwords will have to be recreated as hash used has changed 
- Bugfix: CSV of addresses explorer export via Address Explorere, when account number
  was used, did not reflect the (non-zero) account number.
- Enhancement: Show a progress bar during slow parts of the login process.
- Enhancement: Paper wallet features restored as they were previously. Same cautions apply.
- Last remaining GPL code removed, so licence is now MIT+CC on everything.
```

So this commit, which wired up the entropy bug, was done (at least in part), so they could move off the GNU GPLv3 license, and move instead to MIT+Commons Clause (which prohibits downstream users from selling the software).

# CoinKite's defense

In CoinKite's defense, they argue that the primary reason for migrating to `libNgU` was to use its `libsecp256k1` implementation.

![](https://m.stacker.news/150794)

Whether you find this a plausible explanation or not is up to you. None of us can read the minds and intentions of another. However, I was wondering how defensible the claim was that the move to `libNgU` was motivated primarily by `libsecp256k1`, so I asked Claude.  I won't spoil the response, but if you want you can use the same prompt that I did:

```markdown
Consider this commit in ColdCard's firmware repo: https://github.com/Coldcard/firmware/commit/b18723dddb6d751c39978e4364b56b2414f68b47

The commit message says "First pass w/ libNgU".

The patch notes say both:

- "now using Bitcoin Core's "libsecp256k1" for EC crypto operations"
- "Last remaining GPL code removed, so licence is now MIT+CC on everything"

I know moving to libNgU was partly due to them no longer wanting to use the Trezor libraries so they can move off GPL.  They claim the move was to use libsecp256k1.  

To what extent was moving to libNgU necessary for libsecp256k1?
```

# Conclusion

The reason I said that "the more I look into this, the worse it seems" is because I started to get the feeling that this whole chain of events was set off by NVK wanting to move off of GPLv3, because he felt that someone had unfairly cloned his code, something that he himself had been accused of just 2 years earlier.

Whether or not you think that was the primary trigger is up to you.  I present it only as a possibility.  But by CoinKite's own admission, it was the migration to `libNgU` that wired up the bug on that fateful day of March 1st, 2021.

If anything, it's a good reminder that if you're going to rewire your entire codebase to a new library, you had better do a lot of extra testing before pushing it into production.  And you can't just assume that just because it compiles and runs, that all the same assumptions you made with your previous library would hold.

[^1]: It should be noted that the failure wasn't with `libNgU` itself, but rather with how certain preprocessor directives ColdCard already had in place interacted badly with `libNgU`. You can read more about it all here: [https://engineering.block.xyz/blog/predictable-rng-fallback-and-32-bit-reseed-in-coldcard-firmware](https://engineering.block.xyz/blog/predictable-rng-fallback-and-32-bit-reseed-in-coldcard-firmware)

[^2]: Most of the referenced images in this post come from: [https://www.zherbert.com/an-open-letter-to-nvk-and-coldcard/](https://www.zherbert.com/an-open-letter-to-nvk-and-coldcard/). Note that this article was posted in 2023, long before anyone knew about the entropy bug.

items.title: Bitcoin is my Dread Pirate Roberts
items.text:
# Thank God for Bitcoin influenceoors

The influencer class in bitcoin is looking pretty bad right now...but I never would have learned half as much about Bitcoin without them. The podcasters (many of whom made their bread through sponsorships), the guide-writers, the dev personalities who have so much time for Twitter -- while it is true that [they are all scammers](https://nakamotoinstitute.org/mempool/everyones-a-scammer/), also couldn't help but teach me a little about Bitcoin.

As many bitcoiners describe, when I fell down the Bitcoin rabbit hole there wasn't a podcast I didn't listen to or a guide I didn't read. I tried out every wallet available at the time. I did IBD like seven times because I kept screwing up running an indexer on it and was so bad at computer stuff I didn't know how to keep my blocks data when I needed to try again. Like a child, the only way I could get some things done was if I want back to step zero and tried to follow the steps again. 

For all their attention-grabbing, don't-trust-verify hypocrisy, the clique of bitcoin cool kids managed to get me through a good number of levels. 

So when things like the Coldcard fuckup[^1] come out and all the influencers look like total chumps, I find that I can't be too mad at them because I don't know if I would have really gotten into bitcoin if it weren't for all their "content."

[^1]: I refer to it as the `Coldcard fuckup` because hack is really not the right word and while vulnerability may be the right word, it isn't strong enough.

# My sats aren't stolen yet

I still have my sats, and while I didn't get tripped up by this particular Coldcard blunder, I may end up falling for the next one...or making up one of my own. 

In the course of my time in Bitcoin I have had at least three major incidents where I thought I had completely screwed myself. These were good learning lessons. You can use testnet all you like, but it isn't until you are riding the high seas of mainnet that some things really hit home.

I know that I am not some shadowy supercoder. I'm still quite ignorant about many things in Bitcoin (getting Bitcoin details wrong is still pretty much a daily experience). I often am disappointed with how incredible my Bitcoin ignorance is. But dammit, it's so interesting, I can't seem to focus on anything else!

# Bitcoin is black market money

I've heard it said that Bitcoin may not be for normies, that if you don't need to transact in bitcoin, you probably shouldn't be messing around with it. This is a pretty sobering assessment.

I'm more like a normie than I'd like to admit. I'm a fairly unimportant person who hasn't even bought drugs with bitcoin or something mildly transgressive like that. I live in the US where the financial system works well enough and I can use e-trade if I want. I certainly don't do very much with black markets.

When I transact in bitcoin it's usually because I've gone out of my way to buy a cute coffee or something (well, except that I zap people all day long on SN and I currently don't know of any other platform that provides similar functionality sans sats...). And yet, I can't seem to get past bitcoin.

I don't know if normies should use bitcoin or not, but I still stand by the idea that Bitcoin is for anyone. It's incredibly easy to fuck it up, but if you want to use it, learn about it, try it -- don't let these fuckups stop you. You'll probably do something wrong and make a bunch of mistakes, but what else are you gonna do -- watch the next season of Survivor or something?  

# You don't become the Dread Pirate Roberts by staying home

One of the things that I most enjoyed writing on SN was the [True and Accurate History of Boating Accidents](https://stacker.news/items/869881). The conclusion I drew from researching that meme is that it's not your bitcoin unless you can fuck it up.

Here's something that didn't make it into that piece, but which nicely sums up the way I feel about self custody right now:

In *The Princess Bride* there's this moment where Wesley tells Buttercup about how the Dread Pirate Roberts would say to him every night:

"Goodnight, Wesley. Good work. Sleep well. I'll most likely kill you in the morning."

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aHZGqBVBCRw

Bitcoin is my Dread Pirate Roberts. It may kill me in the morning, but it's been a fine time for me.

> Few political ideas have proven as durable as the complaint embedded in the Declaration of Independence that the British Crown was “imposing taxes on us without our consent.” That grievance was not merely rhetorical flourish; it captured a central concern of the American colonists about the relationship between political authority and individual liberty. More than two centuries later, citizens continue to debate taxation, representation, and accountability, albeit within a vastly different institutional and economic landscape. The question, then, is not whether taxation remains contentious—it clearly does—but whether the underlying concern about consent still has meaningful relevance in contemporary governance.
>
> At first glance, the modern United States appears to have resolved the problem that animated the Revolution. Citizens elect representatives at multiple levels of government, and those representatives possess the constitutional authority to levy taxes. Yet closer examination suggests that the connection between taxation and consent is more complex than formal representation alone. Historical experience, constitutional design, and contemporary fiscal politics all reveal persistent tensions between the ideals of consent and the realities of modern governance.

items.title: Coldcard Mk2, Mk3, Mk4, Mk5, and Q Firmware Security Vulnerability
items.text:
This vulnerability is most severe for RNG generated seeds on Mk2 and Mk3 firmware v4.0.0-v4.1.9, but Mk4 firmware v5.0.0 onward, and all production Q and Mk5 firmware, are also impacted according to Block's report.

If you generated a seed with any of these configurations, and did not generate the seed using dice rolls only, it is recommended to move funds - as soon as you can safely - to another wallet backed with a secure seed. Multisig wallets are also at risk if enough keys were generated on Coldcards and can be recovered to meet its spending threshold. Moving the vulnerable seeds to other devices does nothing. The original seeds are vulnerable so you should generate new ones.

items.title: Trip Report: Chicago
items.text:
When Square [announced Bitcoin Square](https://squareup.com/us/en/press/square-bitcoin) in October of last year, I was hopeful. When I learned how easy it would be to enable, I grew optimistic. I then heard from people who got a chance to use it in the United States, and I became euphoric. However, signing up merchants to enable the feature seemed difficult, and awkward at best. In March 2026, when Square shared its plans to bring this feature as a default to all of it's merchants, I was ecstatic. This July, I finally got the chance to travel to the States to see for myself.

Finding places that take Bitcoin is difficult. I do not have access to the Cash App merchant map, and my understanding is that only those merchants that specifically opted into the Bitcoin trial are listed here. Only a subset of these merchants made it to BTCMap, and while BTCMap volunteers are diligent in adding merchants by request from Square, they will rarely remove a merchant if they move, shut down or stop accepting Bitcoin. My best strategy is to just walk around and rely on the profile of likely Square merchants: Small independent self-service delis, breweries, coffee shops and boutiques with high margins. At these places, I can usually see what checkout terminals they are using from the outside or the door, and I quickly learn how to distinguish them from their doppelgänger toast point of sale.

🛞Detroit: My trip begins in Detroit. A friend recommends a chicken sandwich place by the Eastern Market. It's Saturday, and the market is sprawled and busy. The chicken place however is closed, and I find only one other place with a Square terminal nearby. Bitcoin does not show up as an option on the top left of the screen, and the friendly clerk shows me that it can't be found in the 'Other' options either, although there is a Cash app QR code on the front. I head back to downtown, which looks like a terrible war destroyed most of it seventy years ago, and the city couldn't be rebuilt due to catastrophic collectivist economic policies. I find another place with two Square terminals, an old one and a new one, but neither has the option available, and they also don't have a Cash App option. Finally, at a soft serve ice cream shop with a long line, I peek over the shoulder of somebody paying and notice multiple fingerprints on the top left corner of the screen. I queue and indeed find the Bitcoin option. I have trouble scanning the QR code as the sun shines directly on it, and as I finally succeed and dispatch the payment, the clerk resets the payment screen in an attempt to help me. My payment is rejected, and only as we try a second time I succeed. I held up the line a bit and made the clerk a bit nervous, but I'm glad it worked in the end.

🚆There was one site around 2022 that sold train tickets for Bitcoin, Future Travel. It shut down, and I claim to be the very last person on earth to ever buy a train ticket over Lightning, hopefully not forever. You can however buy Amtrak gift cards on Bitrefill relatively painlessly, and that's what I do for my trip to Chicago.

⛩️My first day in Chicago takes me to Chinatown, where a big festival is held. There are dozens of small merchants, and three of them have handheld Square terminals. We cannot find the Bitcoin option on any of them. I also cannot find a simple merchant advertising their Cash App tag. In the area are lots of small shops selling food, crafts and souvenirs, but nobody seems to have a Square Terminal.

🥽The Riverwalk is probably the best thing to happen to Chicago in the past ten years. I find eight Square merchants in the area, and they all seem to have the latest handheld and tabletop devices, but I can only pay with Bitcoin at two of them. On both screens the Bitcoin and dollar symbols are seen on the top left of the screen. I can tap the ₿ and am then prompted to enter a tipping amount before I'm shown the QR code. I overheard somewhere that this flow would also support "tapping" the NFC antenna to retrieve the Bolt11 invoice, but that does not seem to be true.

🍔There aren't as many Steak & Shake locations in Chicago as there used to be, but there is still one within reach. The experience is absolutely fantastic. There is a special Bitcoin burger on the menu, and paying with Lightning is seamless. The burger is branded with a big ₿, and it tastes quite good, especially for the price (18,584 satoshis plus a 3 satoshi routing fee). There is a claw machine in the room, and I'm sure I could easily Lightningfy that, too.

🏝️Downtown Chicago isn't very lively, not even during the week. I expect my best shot at finding some Square merchants to go to the food courts. The first food court exclusively uses Toast terminals, the second is closed entirely, and the third, at the Willis Tower, seems modern but empty and has one ice cream shop using Square. However, Bitcoin is not available. Around the entire downtown area I can only find five places with Square terminals, including one with a self-service kiosk hooked to a Square handheld device, but Bitcoin isn't available at any of them.

🎩North of the city I find a milk tea place, but the restaurant that I originally come up here for is unexpectedly closed. The donut shop that I found on BTCMap is gone entirely, but there is a soft serve ice cream place nearby where I am lucky to pay with sats. My biggest surprise was Nancy's, a deep dish pizza place where Bitcoin payments were enabled. They had also set a 3% surcharge for card payments, and that charge did not apply to Lightning payments. In this area I also encounter my first real Square self-checkout terminal, which sadly cannot handle Bitcoin payments.

🍸The [Chicago Bitcoin Collective](https://www.chicagobitcoincollective.com/) is a newly established social and co-working space in a quiet neighborhood around Portage Park about half way to the airport. Even if you're just visiting Chicago for a short trip and are interested in meeting Bitcoiners, joining for a single month is very much worth the $25 membership fee. They are preparing to launch a restaurant downstairs, Fork & Coin. This restaurant is also using a Square terminal, including a small handheld device with the form factor of a smart phone. I'm told they have to opt into Bitcoin payments through the admin panel, and I quickly notice how the UI is not as polished, as the device asks for a tip twice, before and after selecting the Bitcoin payment option. A few blocks away there is a Mexican restaurant "Migos Fine Foods." They also have a self-service kiosk connected to a handheld Square terminal that does not take Bitcoin, but I succeed at the counter.

🪙There are a few Bitcoin ATMs around town, according to CoinATMRadar, but I only find one, a two-way operated by Rockitcoin. It requires me to register with a phone number to just show me the rate (a transparent 14% premium over the market rate to sell BTC), and requires me to scan a U.S. driver's license. I also check out a Coinstar machine, but it seems their Bitcoin integration is gone.

All together I found 24 Square merchants on my trip, 7 of which had Bitcoin payments enabled on their devices. Whenever I saw the ₿ symbol at the top left of the screen, payments were a breeze. I made nine payments, all of which went through within a few seconds, for between a 0.015 and 0.025% routing fee, virtually free. Square deserves a lot of praise for the solution they have come up with, even if it is not available at all locations. I wish Square could manage the data of their merchants on OpenStreetMaps better, which BTCMaps is based on. This would be a benefit to all their merchants, not just Bitcoin, and could even give them a small competitive advantage over competitors, as many Square merchants weren't found on OpenStreetMaps at all, or only with outdated opening hours or contact information.

It takes some imagination to see how all of this is supposed to come together. All Cash App users can supposedly pay the Lightning invoices shown on Square Terminals, but they have little incentive to do so, and more importantly, they likely don't know this option exists.

I'm personally strongly of the opinion that Lightning would be better branding than Bitcoin in this case. After all, Lightning is a payment protocol, and Bitcoin is a currency. We don't advertise which currencies we accept (you generally don't see "We accept USD" stickers in the U.S.), but rather what payment methods we process ("Cash and card accepted here"). Similarly, businesses would advertise "Lightning payments accepted here," and a Cash App user and Square merchant both holding U.S. dollars in their account would have no confusion over why they are going through a separate currency they both might not want. Additionally, I think Lightning has great branding, wonderful symbols that cannot be patented, it's easily translatable into all languages and doesn't carry awkward connotations.

I hope that we are going to see more businesses joining Square, upgrading their devices or opting into Lightning payments. I hope Cash App users learn they can pay from their app directly, rather than going through their cards, and I hope they financially benefit from paying with Lightning over card. Eventually Lightning will succeed over stable coins and card networks because it is an open system, that competitors like Toast and Venmo can freely integrate into their systems.

items.title: Pleb Economist #13: ColdCard and the Law of Large Numbers
items.text:
This recent ColdCard incident highlighted a vulnerability in Bitcoin that we always knew about---weak entropy---but it also reminded me of a more subtle weakness, a weakness that I also consider to be the biggest vulnerability in the entire discipline of economics.

And that's reliance on the **Law of Large Numbers**.

I remarked in https://stacker.news/items/1536440/r/SimpleStacker?commentId=1536680 that one of the **security assumptions** that made me feel comfortable using popular and seasoned hardware wallets is the notion that "if there was a major flaw, it would have been discovered by now."  It's on that assumption that I'm willing to adopt things that are popular and have been around for a while, and also why I'm slow to update.  The older version is more battle-tested, in my mind.

But the ColdCard scenario tests that assumption.  The vulnerability, once explained, is not that hard to understand (https://stacker.news/items/1536739/r/SimpleStacker).  The software had an if/else conditional that took the seed generation down the wrong path, never calling for hardware generation which uses noise in the physical environment, and instead falling back to its pre-defined, low-entropy software generation.  The question is **how did no one catch it for so long?**

The answer has to be: [not enough people were actually looking at it](https://stacker.news/items/1536478/r/SimpleStacker?commentId=1536686).  Bitcoin is a small community, and everyone is busy with their own things.  Very few people are spending the time to audit code.  You'd think the company has the responsibility, *and it does*, but the company itself probably only has a handful of engineers, all of whom are also busy, and if internal processes aren't correct, then these things can easily slip through the cracks.

Make no mistake though, this definitely looks like a failure on ColdCard's part.  Personally, I can't imagine not having a test to actually test whether the build is pulling entropy from physical signals, and whether the firmware actually routed the seed generation down the correct path.

But I digress.  The point is that, a lot of assumptions that we make rely on a critical mass of people actually doing something that you'd think they're incentivized to do.  But that's often not a good assumption.  Even if the incentive is there, there may be fewer people doing it than you think, at any given moment.

It's the same thing in economics. The classical arguments for why competitive markets are efficient rely on the Law of Large Numbers. They assume that there are enough people out there competing that bad actors can't get away with their bad actions for long.  Company is out there scamming customers or providing bad product?  Economists assume that there are thousands of potential competitors out there ready to jump into the opening left by the terrible company.  But reality isn't so simple.  At any given moment, you could probably count on one hand the number of people paying enough attention, and with enough capital and know-how to actually fill the gap.

Same with the Efficient Market Hypothesis. That's the idea that you can't beat the market, because the market price of any security on the stock market already contains all the relevant information.  But how true is that, really?  It's probably a decent approximation for heavily traded ETF baskets; but probably not for individual companies, especially smaller ones.  For those, there are likely a small number of people with better information who haven't acted on it yet, perhaps waiting for an opportune moment, or perhaps just having not spent their attention on it just yet.

This way of thinking has led to the classic joke: "Milton Friedman and Eugene Fama are walking down the street. Friedman sees a hundred dollar bill on the floor and says, 'Look, Eugene, someone left a hundred dollar bill!'  Fama, without looking down, says, 'Nonsense! If there was a hundred dollar bill lying around, someone would have taken it alraedy!'"

So you see, assumptions that everyone is always relentless optimizing at any moment, and that there are enough people out there doing rational things that all the rational things always get done instantly, is generally not a very good assumption.  Yet, economists rely on it for their models.  And, more relevant for this crowd: Bitcoiners can sometimes rely on it for their security assumptions.

It comes into play when Bitcoiners address questions about things like nation state attacks, like in this [famous Antonopoulos video](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/P3K70rkaCJc).  He assumes that we don't have to worry about a nation state attack because enough Bitcoiners will be ready to respond to it properly, and in a coordinated fashion.  He's right that if we did respond this way, it wouldn't be a huge concern.  But would we really be able to?  Will enough people be paying attention?  The nation state attacker would probably run enough psyops to seed doubt in the community as to what's really going on.  The number of actors prepared to act in their best interest at any given moment may be smaller than you think.

So that's the point I was trying to make.  Bitcoin relies on game theoretic security.  Game theoretic security relies on assumptions about how people behave according to their incentives.  No one denies that people *do* act according to their incentives.  But most game theoretic models assume a level of rationality that just isn't realistic.  Most people are not paying attention all the time.  The number of people who will act according to the model at any given moment is probably small.  The model may predict directions of movement over time fairly well, but "predicting direction over time" is not a good rubric with which to measure security.

In that sense, even though the ColdCard incident is a failure of the company, not Bitcoin, it also calls into question how we should think about macrosecurity in the Bitcoin system as a whole.

items.title: The Forest Reunion - How I lost my passion for music.
items.text:
The following probably shares more personal information about parts of my life than the reader may care to know. I'm sharing this as I wrote it as an honest attempt to strengthen the conviction of a potentially tired or jaded reader who believes in, and works toward bitcoin adoption for similar reasons to myself: freedom from unnecessary human control. I'm not quite sure how to make it less personal, and as this post will reveal, I don't reject all authority as a concept outright. Please be forewarned as, to some, either of those inclusions will certainly be more nauseating than the post if helpful, and I do value your time.

# I got a rejection letter yesterday

It stung so hard. I am pretty sure that I know exactly why I lost this particular opportunity. It was the end of the second interview and the panel asked, "Can you think of a time when you enforced a policy you disagreed with? How did that play out? We're a highly regulated company and we have to enforce many policies involving KYC rules and other legal compliance."

This should have been my clincher moment. I was uncharacteristically nervous though. My phone (despite actually being plugged in) had just died, interrupting the interview for more than a couple of minutes, and I was feeling tense. I reached in my mind for a period of time in which I enforced a policy that I disagreed with.

The following story is **NOT** how I lost my passion for music.

# Covid

In late 2015, after much of my artistic and touring career had been on hold for a few years, I started a branch of a corporate party band company in a midwestern city. I recruited and trained a couple hundred musicians while also booking and managing a few events a month in another established city about two hours away. By the end of the year, I was booking and managing thirty or more events a month in the new city. That following year, I was tasked with bringing order to another neighboring city a few hours away in which the person in my position had been asked to step down. This experience was brutal, as I came in under high suspicion by the musicians, venues, and other vendors alike. For quite a while, everyone there was hostile. Within about a year and a half, that city was doing as well as mine.

When Covid struck, I was supposed to be on my first true, "do-not-contact," vacation in half a decade, yet I spent the first week harshly enforcing contracts, what I still believe was the correct call. This meant that the client was out of a 20% deposit, no small chunk of change, even for the wealthiest people in society. Nevertheless, it's how we protected our musicians, many with families and typically not the wealthiest people in society if they're working the wedding band circuits.

What I shared with my interviewers last week was what started with a phone call in the Denver airport in March of 2020. Despite building their business in a large swath of the midwest, I was instructed by my superiors to enforce **their** new policy about Covid related cancellations.

* First off, we are pausing all cancellation payouts for musicians. I was livid, but there was a silver lining. At least all of these high net worth people that had been yelling at me on the phone the last few days of my "vacation" would get their money and peace of mind back.
* Second off...well you probably already guessed it. We're still keeping the deposits.

So here I am, having made this company millions, enforcing the worst of both worlds. We're keeping the deposits despite the crazy circumstances and breaking our contracts with our contractors, despite our agreements to pay out some fees for cancellations. All this, despite my having built them an operation in the region that had made millions by this point. I made my opinion heard, gritted my teeth while enforcing this policy, and finally trained a few people to replace me after a few months.

# The exact wrong response

So last week I said some platitudes about living in the real world and ended with this depressing tale, portraying myself as a pushover and a quitter. Both of these preparatives are, of course, accurate. But I still think my decisions reflected both my recognition of the proper need for authority and also the integrity to hold the line in the least destructive manner possible. Simply put, my track record trends toward radical, but not for the sake of being radical. I believe last week that I expressed the exact opposite of this in the way I framed this story.

# Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)

Wedding bands are fun. When done right, they're very lucrative. That said, if I never...**ever** hear September, Uptown Funk, Don't Stop Believing, Shake it off, or Crazy in Love again, I'll be just fine. No one ever picked up a guitar with starry-eyed dreams of playing some rich guy's daughter's third wedding. 

But this also is **NOT** how I lost my passion for music.

I actually *really* fell in love with music when I first discovered jazz. Real jazz! Have you ever heard Rahsaan Roland Kirk, Kenny Garrett, John Coltrane, Bill Frisell, Sonny Rollins, Chick Corea, McCoy Tyner, Woody Shaw, Steve Turre, Jaco Pastorious, Curtis Fuller, Pat Metheny, Albert Ayler, Bela Fleck, Courtney Pine, Chris Potter, Eddie Bayard, Paul Brown, Andy Woodson, James Gaiters, Chris Howes, Bobby Floyd, or Derek DiCenzo?! There are so many more. What's even more amazing is that there used to be a pretty strong economy built around this music, and more recently than many here may realize. In the decades before doing the wedding band thing, I spent about half my time performing R\&B (often on the road), but about half my time performing jazz, including with some of my musical heroes listed above.

That economy went away at one point. I had to pivot towards less adventurous musical endeavors. 

But that's also **NOT** how I lost my passion for music.

# How I lost my passion for music

I still love music, and it's how I pay the bills to this day, but you may have gathered already from this post that it's not how I hope to. And I've been trying to make that transition for a while.

A few years back, I was sitting in a club waiting to perform with an "avant garde" jazz ensemble. It paid ostensibly nothing, but there was a really talented "jazz famous" guy sitting in with our group that night and I was kind of excited. The club also gave us all a free burrito and chips. :)

Half way through my chips, some part of my brain heard something that made me pay attention to the conversation at the next table. A member of the band who had a doctorate in "jazz studies" was speaking with our guest artist. He had just been hired by a prestigious university and was describing his curriculum plans. The guest artist made a passing comment about how it sounds like he's institutionalizing jazz music, and the phd guy retorted, "well isn't that the point?"

This was the exact moment that I decided that I want to work in any capacity toward making Bitcoin more successful and accessible. I still enjoy music much more than the average bear, but the sentiment expressed by the phd guy is the exact opposite of what compelled me to tens of thousands of hours of practice back in the day. And it's far from the minority view at this point. Listen to any of my musical heroes listed above and, potentially, the only common thread you'll hear is a lack of institutional rule following. But the youngest of those folks is now the old guard.

It's no coincidence that jazz music originates from, and traditionally thrives in the black community. It is rebel music at it's core. The joy of Louis Armstrong, the complexities of Charlie Parker, and the freedom of Ornette Coleman all establish loose structures (even authority) in an effort to cast aside oppressive control. But "jazz studies" is now a part of normal university curriculum, and despite the standards being way lower than what's necessary to even play cheap bar gigs, the power to codify the rules is established and enforced. I wouldn't go so far as to say, "jazz is dead," but it sure ain't what it used to be...

Furthermore, and more importantly, I found another way to scratch that itch.

# Spoiler Alert (not clickbait)

I'm reading The Two Towers to my two daughters right now. The night after my terminal interview with this bitcoin company, a scene I had long forgot underscored the motivations behind my attempted transitions the last few years and my failure that day at the same time. (last warning, the sentence after next is a huge spoiler) The scene is the forest reunion. Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli are all reunited with a Gandalf they long thought dead.

As a quick aside, the reunion starts with a mesmerizingly beautiful conversation about Boromir's last day in Middle Earth in which Gandalf is relieved to hear he "escaped." It's a stunning theological lesson about grace, and an example of one of my favorite things about Tolkien's writing. I've long thought that Tolkien is so much more popular with the secular community than his friend C.S. Lewis because all of his preaching goes over all of our heads. Setting aside their essays, and only focusing on the fiction, I'm convinced that Lewis writes philosophy disguised as narrative while Tolkien writes narrative disguised as philosophy. As a result, when reading the former, we bump into offense and sometimes miss a brilliant tale. But when reading the latter, we go on an adventure, and suddenly that amputation on Mount Doom is less than a quarter as exciting (and offensive) as it really should be. I digress.

After confusing the three of them with this speech about Boromir, Gandalf then continues to catch up with another "riddle," to borrow Aragorn's description.

> 'What then shall I say?' said Gandalf, and paused for a while in thought. 'This in brief is how I see things at the moment, if you wish to have a piece of my mind as plain as possible. The Enemy, of course, long has known that the ring is abroad, and that it is borne by a hobbit. He knows now the number of our Company that set out from Rivendell, and the kind of each of us. But he does not yet see our purpose clearly. He supposed that we were all going to Minas Tirith; for that is what he himself would have done in our place. And according to his wisdom it would have been a heavy stroke against his power. Indeed he is in great fear, not knowing what mighty one may suddenly appear, wielding the ring, and assailing his with war, seeking to cast him down and take his place. That we should wish to cast him down and have *no* (emphasis Gandalf's, not mine) one in his place is not a thought that occurs to his mind. That we should try to destroy the ring itself has not yet entered into his darkest dream. In which no doubt you will see our good fortune and our hope. For imagining war he has let lose war, believing that he has no time to waste; for he that strikes the first blow, if he strikes it hard enough, may need to strike no more. So the forces that he has long been preparing he is now setting in motion, sooner than he intended. Wise fool. For if he had used all his power to guard Mordor, so that none could enter, and bent all his guile on the hunting of the Ring, then indeed hope would have faded: neither Ring nor bearer could have long eluded him. But now his eye gazes abroad rather than near at home; and mostly he looks toward Minas Tirith. Very soon now his strength will fall upon it like a storm.'

I have no memory of reading this part as a kid.

I had long remembered the theme throughout this epic that the free peoples of Middle Earth all had to put aside their differences and band together if they wanted to continue their individual ways of life. I've even long enjoyed the funny, annoyed responses Tolkien is recorded giving when people said it was an allegory for either of the world wars since that theme is so similar. But somehow, over the years, I forgot that part of the success of the free people in the Lord of the Rings is the fact that Sauron doesn't even have a **category** for them not wanting someone in charge.

Read that Gandalf quote again and tell me with a straight face that Tolkien wouldn't have been a bitcoiner!

What's wild is that I asked the LLMs about this, and they came up with a totally different passage! "You must be remembering the council of Elrond." Sure enough, I checked and he outlines the same strategy, as well as the enemies same oversight thereof in the first book. I didn't just miss it as a kid, I missed it again when I read it to my girls last month. But it's there, and I think I caught it last Wednesday because of my flub. This is a major theme of the book. Freedom loving people want to minimize human power over others, and the most power-hungry don't even have a category for someone not wanting that power themselves.

# Delegated Authority

I know this is stacker news, and there are a number of folks that I respect here that don't respect those of us that believe authority has a place at all. But I'm in good company. There's no doubt that Tolkien believed in authority. The man was Roman Catholic. Elrond rightly leads the counsel, Gandalf responsibly leads the Fellowship, and ultimately, Aragorn justly leads his country. Yet, he's not as black and white about most moral issues as he's often portrayed. It wasn't enough to keep the ring from Sauron. It wasn't enough to keep the ring from Saruman. It didn't just tempt Boromir. It didn't just take Frodo. The ring was good for **NO MAN**. It's what I loved about jazz. It's what I love about bitcoin. Just like Sauron, the enemies of bitcoin think it's about moving power elsewhere. They have no idea that it might be about removing a whole layer of power altogether. It's why so much of my passion has been sucked into something so seemingly different from what I've spent most of my life doing.

# The response next time

> I believe we need to be radical. But we also need to be effective. Bitcoiners love Hayek's famous, "sly trick" quote, but in practice we are anything but sly when dealing with the uninitiated. I want to do something radical, and I'm convinced this company is doing something radical. I want to see a more fair, just, and prospering world, but I don't think we get there with chaos. I believe in freedom **and** authority. When authority is abused, I don't jump to chaos as a response, but I want to fight alongside and for people that reject needless control. Now that we have bitcoin, needless control is what the dollar has become. I would like to be with an organization that is working towards dissolving that control.

# The cross comes before the crown and tomorrow is a Monday morning!

The above quote is from Tolkien's friend C.S. Lewis. He's talking about even loftier ideas in the essay quoted (The Weight of Glory), but the point applies to this work as well. The past seven months have been pretty depressing for me. After going whole hog on trying to setup a bitcoin project last year, I'm back to playing local gigs. Sometimes it's so joyful. That's what the best music always is. Sometimes it's work. That's good too. But a lot of what I've worked so hard for has been consumed pursuing "bitcoin stuff." Maybe you've had setbacks too. If you have, I hope you remember what's so exciting about the opportunity this technology presents. If bitcoin succeeds in the manner that many on this forum hope it will:

**No one will be in control of the money.**

That's not just a clever approach that breaks the rules. That's something that will change people's lives. Maybe I won't ever get my bitcoin job. There are plenty of ways outside of a job to pursue this end. There are also other noble pursuits (some greater) which we should pursue as well. But that's a darn good one.
